newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks seen sucking money from faded gold.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks seen sucking money from faded gold.

text.p: Money quitting a jaundiced gold market contributed to Indian stocks bull run this week, but there was no indication of a huge and sustained move, brokers and analysts said on Friday.
A wave of foreign funds drawn to India by attractive valuations has been the most common factor cited for the Bombay stock market's leap to 33-month highs this week.
But analysts also pointed to a clutch of domestic factors along with gold's fall to a 12-year low as reasons behind the buoyant stock market.

Lower property prices, reduced bank deposit rates and the high-profile collapse of a non-bank finance house (NBFC), which knocked confidence in these alternative high interest rate deposit firms, have all played a part, they said.
"A lot of players have entered the market," said broker Ashok Agarwal, a former president of the Delhi Stock Exchange.

"There is the fact that new projects are not being set up, the fact that property prices and gold prices are going down... Money from all these sources have started getting attracted to the capital market," Agarwal told Reuters.
Bombay's benchmark 30-share index rose to a 33-month high of 4,448.06 on Wednesday, and paused on Friday, when it was trading around 4307.77, down from Thursday's close of 4,378.37.
A key cause spurring the rise was a delayed response to an attractive budget presented earlier this year, analysts said.
Gold tumbled sharply worldwide to 12-year-lows below $325 an ounce after the Australian central bank announced last week it had sold off 167 tonnes of its gold reserves.

Agarwal said a poor initial public offering (IPO) demand and high borrowing rates of around 17.5 percent had stalled many Indian industrial projects. "A lot of money finding no other use are entering the stock market," he said.
India's IPO and real estate markets have been running low, linked to an IPO shake-out and high interest rates.

"Gold was definitely in the stock market but now it has starting coming back. The stocks have increased partly because of gold money," said Shree Krishna Goel, a bullion merchant. He said funds were switched to stocks from gold much earlier.
Analysts felt the pro-market Indian budget presented earlier this year was a key factor driving stocks. They said the main liquidity came from foreign institutional investors (FIIs).
"Most of the money came in from FIIs," broker Rattan Singhania said. "I think subject to technical corrections, it will last."

"The budget was excellent, but the market had not given it enough credence because of political uncertainties," investment analyst and merchant banker P.N. Vijay, managing director of P.N. Vijay Financial Services Pvt Ltd, told Reuters.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram slashed corporate and personal tax rates in the budget for 1997/98 (April-March).

The budget was presented on February 28, but only passed in May after Prime Minister Inder Gujral took over leadership of the United Front government from H.D. Deve Gowda -- who was ousted by the Congress party in April.
Vijay said bank deposit rates had begun dropping following central bank initiatives, spurring a shift in investment to stocks by depositors who found bank interest rates unattractive.
But the rally was mainly spurred by foreign funds buying up the bluest of blue chips, he added.

"Large FIIs have come in to the market," Vijay said. "They are going for real blue chips. They have been buying branded companies, multinational stocks especially. They are not touching Indian stocks. They are going for quality at a price."

Vijay said the failure some weeks ago of CRB Capital Markets, a non-banking financial company, had shaken the confidence of depositors in such firms. But he was less sure about an exodus of money from precious metals or real estate.
"I don't think gold and property money is coming in. People feel it may come. With lowering of interest rates, it may come."
--New Delhi newsroom (91) 11 301 2024
